_comment: 500-entry dataset of atomic technical/causal claims extracted primarily from well-known ML/AI research papers. Lighter schema than the physics propositions.json (no formal context/MONOTONIC_* apparatus) -- this is a paper-claim extraction dataset, not a formal K-IR benchmark, though the same 'one atomic idea per entry, cite the source' discipline applies. Building in batches; see README.md for progress and schema.

entries.paper: Vaswani et al. 2017 (Attention Is All You Need)
entries.claim: The Transformer architecture replaces recurrence entirely with self-attention for sequence modeling.
Scaled dot-product attention divides QK^T by sqrt(d_k) before softmax, preventing large-magnitude dot products from pushing softmax into low-gradient saturation regions.
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel on different learned linear projections of Q/K/V, letting the model attend to different representation subspaces simultaneously.
Sinusoidal positional encodings inject sequence-order information into token embeddings because self-attention itself is permutation-invariant.
Self-attention computes pairwise interactions between all token pairs, costing O(n^2) time and memory in sequence length n.
Residual connections around each Transformer sub-layer, combined with layer normalization, stabilize training of deep Transformer stacks.
The Transformer decoder uses masked self-attention so a position cannot attend to future positions during autoregressive generation.
Cross-attention in encoder-decoder Transformers lets decoder queries attend to encoder key/value pairs, connecting source and target sequences.
BERT uses a bidirectional Transformer encoder pretrained with masked language modeling and next-sentence prediction.
GPT uses a unidirectional (causal) Transformer decoder pretrained by next-token prediction.
Scaling a causal Transformer language model up in parameters and training data improves its zero-shot task performance.
A sufficiently large autoregressive language model can perform few-shot learning from examples placed in the prompt, without any gradient updates.
T5 reframes every NLP task as text-to-text and trains a single encoder-decoder Transformer on this unified format.
The Vision Transformer applies a standard Transformer encoder to a sequence of image patches instead of using convolutions.
FlashAttention reduces the memory and wall-clock cost of exact attention by fusing operations and avoiding materializing the full attention matrix in slow GPU memory.
Rotary position embeddings encode relative position information by rotating query and key vectors as a function of token position.
Relative position representations let attention scores depend on the relative distance between tokens rather than only absolute position.
Sparse attention patterns restrict each token to attend to a limited set of positions, reducing the quadratic cost of full self-attention for long sequences.
Layer normalization is the standard normalization used inside Transformer blocks because, unlike batch normalization, it does not depend on batch statistics.
Applying layer normalization before each sub-layer (Pre-LN), rather than after (Post-LN), trains more stably at greater Transformer depth.
Stochastic Gradient Descent updates parameters using the gradient estimated from a small random mini-batch rather than the full dataset, trading gradient accuracy for computational efficiency.
Momentum accumulates an exponentially decaying moving average of past gradients to accelerate convergence and dampen oscillation in narrow loss-surface valleys.
Nesterov accelerated gradient evaluates the gradient at a momentum-adjusted look-ahead point rather than the current position, improving convergence over classical momentum.
AdaGrad adapts each parameter's learning rate by dividing by the square root of the sum of its past squared gradients, giving infrequently-updated parameters larger effective steps.
AdaGrad's accumulated squared-gradient denominator grows monotonically, causing its effective learning rate to shrink toward zero over long training runs.
RMSProp fixes AdaGrad's vanishing-learning-rate problem by using an exponentially decaying moving average of squared gradients instead of a cumulative sum.
Adam combines a momentum-style first moment estimate with an RMSProp-style adaptive second moment estimate, plus bias correction for both.
Adam's bias-correction terms compensate for its moment estimates being initialized at zero, which would otherwise bias early-training updates toward zero.
AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient-based update, applying it directly to the weights instead of folding it into the gradient as plain Adam with L2 regularization does.

entries.paper: Common practice; e.g. Vaswani et al. 2017
entries.claim: Learning-rate warmup gradually increases the learning rate from a small value at training start, stabilizing early training of large models like Transformers.
Cosine learning-rate decay anneals the learning rate along a cosine curve toward a minimum over training, often combined with periodic warm restarts.
Gradient clipping caps the norm of gradients before the parameter update, preventing exploding gradients from destabilizing training, especially in RNNs.
LAMB extends Adam-style updates with per-layer adaptive learning-rate scaling based on the ratio of weight norm to update norm, enabling stable large-batch training.
Linear learning-rate scaling with batch size preserves training dynamics when using large-batch data-parallel training.

Second-order optimization methods use curvature information (an approximation to the Hessian or Fisher information matrix) to precondition gradient updates, at higher per-step compute cost than first-order methods.
Adam's default hyperparameters beta1=0.9 and beta2=0.999 set the decay rates of its first and second moment moving averages respectively.
Weight decay penalizes the squared norm of the weights, encouraging smaller weights and acting as a form of L2 regularization.
A learning-rate decay phase is used because a constant rate large enough for fast early progress is typically too large to allow convergence to a sharp minimum late in training.
Lookahead maintains slow-moving anchor weights that periodically pull toward fast weights updated by an inner optimizer, improving training stability.
Sharpness-Aware Minimization seeks parameters in flat regions of the loss landscape by minimizing the worst-case loss within a neighborhood of current weights, improving generalization.
Dropout randomly zeroes a fraction of unit activations during training, preventing co-adaptation of neurons and acting as an implicit ensemble of subnetworks.
At test time, dropout is disabled, with activations scaled (inverted dropout) to match the expected magnitude seen during training.
Batch normalization normalizes layer activations using the mean and variance computed over each mini-batch, then applies a learned scale and shift.
Batch normalization's main empirical benefit is smoothing the optimization landscape, not reducing internal covariate shift as originally proposed by Ioffe & Szegedy.
Batch normalization's statistics depend on batch composition, making it less effective with very small batch sizes or online/streaming training.
Layer normalization normalizes across the feature dimension for each example rather than across the batch, making it independent of batch size.
Weight decay (L2 regularization) biases the optimizer toward simpler models with smaller parameter values.
Early stopping halts training when validation loss stops improving, preventing the model from continuing to fit noise in the training data after the point of best generalization.
Label smoothing replaces hard one-hot classification targets with a mixture of the one-hot target and a uniform distribution, discouraging over-confident predictions.
Data augmentation artificially expands the effective training set via label-preserving transformations, improving generalization.
Mixup trains on convex combinations of pairs of training examples and their labels, encouraging the model to behave linearly between training examples.

Stochastic depth randomly drops entire residual layers during training while keeping the identity shortcut, reducing effective network depth per step and improving generalization in very deep ResNets.
DropConnect generalizes dropout by randomly zeroing individual weights (connections) rather than whole unit activations.
Cutout regularizes CNN training for images by masking out random contiguous square regions of the input during training.
Spectral normalization constrains the largest singular value of each weight matrix, stabilizing GAN discriminator training by enforcing an approximate Lipschitz constraint.
WGAN-GP's gradient penalty term penalizes deviation of the discriminator's gradient norm from 1, enforcing an approximate Lipschitz constraint without weight clipping.
Ensembling multiple independently trained models and averaging their predictions typically improves generalization over any single model, at extra training and inference cost.
Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to match the softened output distribution of a larger teacher model, rather than only hard labels.

Batch normalization's learned scale and shift parameters let the network recover the original unnormalized representation if that is optimal, so normalization does not reduce representational capacity.
Elastic Weight Consolidation regularizes continual learning by penalizing changes to parameters that were important for previously learned tasks, mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
LeNet-5 combines convolution, subsampling (pooling), and fully connected layers for handwritten digit recognition, an early convolutional architecture.
AlexNet showed that a deep CNN trained on GPUs with ReLU activations and dropout dramatically outperformed prior methods on ImageNet classification.
ReLU activations avoid the vanishing-gradient problem of saturating activations like sigmoid/tanh for positive inputs, a key factor in AlexNet's success.
Stacking many small 3x3 convolution filters achieves a larger effective receptive field with fewer parameters than fewer large filters, while adding non-linearity between them.
Inception modules apply multiple filter sizes (1x1, 3x3, 5x5) in parallel within the same layer and concatenate their outputs.
1x1 convolutions in Inception modules reduce channel dimensionality as a bottleneck before more expensive larger convolutions, cutting computational cost.
ResNet's residual (skip) connections let a layer learn a residual function relative to its input, mitigating vanishing gradients and enabling training of networks over 100 layers deep.
Before ResNet, simply stacking more layers in plain CNNs was empirically observed to increase training error, the 'degradation problem' that residual connections address.
DenseNet connects each layer to every other layer in a feed-forward fashion within a block, encouraging feature reuse and alleviating vanishing gradients.
Batch normalization is commonly placed after convolution and before the non-linearity in CNN blocks, stabilizing and accelerating training.

entries.paper: He et al. 2015 (ResNet); Lin et al. 2013 (NiN)
entries.claim: Global average pooling reduces each feature map to a single value by averaging, cutting parameter count and reducing overfitting compared to flattening plus dense layers.
MobileNet uses depthwise separable convolutions -- a depthwise spatial convolution followed by a pointwise 1x1 convolution -- to reduce computation for mobile/embedded deployment.
EfficientNet's compound scaling method jointly scales network depth, width, and input resolution according to a fixed ratio found via neural architecture search.
U-Net's encoder-decoder CNN uses skip connections between corresponding encoder and decoder layers, preserving fine spatial detail for pixel-level tasks like segmentation.
Faster R-CNN's Region Proposal Network shares convolutional features with the detection head, making object proposal generation nearly cost-free compared to earlier two-stage detectors.
YOLO reframes object detection as a single regression problem, directly predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities from a full image in one forward pass, trading some accuracy for speed.
Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN by adding a parallel branch that predicts a segmentation mask for each detected object, alongside classification and box regression.
Squeeze-and-Excitation blocks adaptively reweight channel-wise feature responses using a learned per-channel gating mechanism, improving representational power at low extra cost.
Dilated (atrous) convolutions increase a convolution's receptive field without increasing parameter count or reducing spatial resolution, by inserting gaps between kernel elements.
CNNs pretrained on large datasets like ImageNet and fine-tuned on a smaller target dataset typically outperform training from random initialization when target data is limited.
Recurrent Neural Networks process sequences by maintaining a hidden state updated at each time step as a function of the current input and the previous hidden state.

entries.paper: Bengio et al. 1994; Pascanu et al. 2013
entries.claim: Vanilla RNNs suffer from vanishing and exploding gradients over long sequences because gradients are repeatedly multiplied by the same recurrent weight matrix during backpropagation through time.
The LSTM's memory cell with input, forget, and output gates lets gradients flow through many time steps largely unattenuated, mitigating vanishing gradients.
The LSTM forget gate learns to decide how much of the previous cell state to retain versus discard at each time step.
The Gated Recurrent Unit simplifies the LSTM by merging the cell and hidden state and using two gates (reset and update) instead of three, with fewer parameters.
Sequence-to-sequence models use an encoder RNN to compress an input sequence into a fixed-size vector and a decoder RNN to generate an output sequence from that vector.
A fixed-size context vector in vanilla seq2seq models creates an information bottleneck that degrades performance on long input sequences, motivating attention mechanisms.
Bahdanau attention lets the decoder at each output step compute a weighted combination of all encoder hidden states, rather than relying on a single fixed context vector.
Luong attention introduced simpler global and local attention scoring functions, such as dot-product, as alternatives to Bahdanau's additive attention.
Bidirectional RNNs process a sequence in both forward and backward directions and combine the resulting hidden states, giving each position access to both past and future context.

Teacher forcing trains sequence generation models by feeding the ground-truth previous token as input at each decoding step, speeding up training but causing train/inference mismatch known as exposure bias.
Beam search decoding keeps the top-k highest-scoring partial sequences at each generation step, exploring more of the output space than greedy decoding at added computational cost.
Truncated backpropagation through time limits gradient computation to a fixed number of past time steps, trading exact gradients for tractable memory and compute on long sequences.
ELMo produces contextualized word representations from the internal states of a bidirectional LSTM language model, so a word's embedding depends on its surrounding context.
Connectionist Temporal Classification allows training sequence models, such as for speech recognition, without requiring exact frame-level alignment between input and output sequences.
Peephole connections let LSTM gates observe the cell state directly, rather than only the previous hidden state, improving modeling of precise timing.
Stacked multi-layer RNNs pass the hidden-state sequence of one recurrent layer as input to the next, letting the model learn hierarchical temporal representations.
RNN-based language models estimate the probability of a token conditioned on all previous tokens by recursively updating a hidden state, factorizing sequence probability via the chain rule.
Gradient clipping is especially important when training RNNs because exploding gradients are common from repeated multiplication through the recurrent weight matrix over many time steps.
Attention mechanisms originally developed for RNN-based seq2seq models were later shown to be sufficient on their own, without recurrence, giving rise to the Transformer.
word2vec learns dense word vectors by training a shallow network to predict context words from a target word (skip-gram) or the target word from context (CBOW).

Skip-gram with negative sampling approximates the full softmax over the vocabulary by training the model to distinguish true context words from randomly sampled negative examples, making training tractable at scale.
GloVe learns word vectors by factorizing a global word-word co-occurrence count matrix, combining global corpus statistics with the local-context intuition of word2vec.
Word embeddings trained on large corpora capture semantic relationships such that vector arithmetic, e.g. king minus man plus woman, often approximates real-world analogies like queen.
Static word embeddings like word2vec and GloVe assign a single fixed vector to each word type, unable to represent different meanings of a word depending on context (polysemy).
ELMo produces contextualized embeddings where the same word receives different vector representations depending on its surrounding sentence.
BERT's WordPiece tokenization splits rare or unknown words into common subword units, letting the model represent an open vocabulary with a fixed-size vocabulary table.
BERT's [CLS] token representation from the final layer is commonly used as an aggregate sequence representation for classification tasks.
BERT's masked language modeling objective randomly masks a percentage of input tokens and trains the model to predict them from bidirectional context.
GPT-style causal language models cannot use future tokens to predict the current token, unlike BERT's bidirectional masked language modeling.
Byte-Pair Encoding builds a subword vocabulary by iteratively merging the most frequent adjacent symbol pairs observed in a training corpus.
RoBERTa showed that BERT was undertrained, and that training longer, with more data, larger batches, and removing the next-sentence-prediction objective improved downstream performance.
ALBERT reduces BERT's parameter count via factorized embedding parameterization and cross-layer parameter sharing, without a proportional loss in performance.
DistilBERT uses knowledge distillation to train a smaller Transformer that retains most of BERT's performance with fewer parameters and faster inference.
Sentence-BERT fine-tunes Transformer encoders with a siamese/triplet-loss objective so that embedding cosine similarity reflects semantic sentence similarity.
BERT's next-sentence-prediction pretraining objective was shown by RoBERTa to be unnecessary or even harmful for many downstream tasks.
Byte-level BPE operates on raw bytes rather than Unicode characters, guaranteeing that any input text can be tokenized without out-of-vocabulary tokens.
Contextualized embeddings from deep pretrained language models generally outperform static word embeddings on downstream NLP tasks because they capture context-dependent meaning.
An embedding layer is a learned lookup table mapping discrete tokens, such as word or subword IDs, to dense continuous vectors.
Tying a language model's input embedding weights to its output softmax projection weights reduces parameter count and often improves performance.

A Generative Adversarial Network trains a generator and a discriminator in a minimax game, where the generator learns to produce samples indistinguishable from real data and the discriminator learns to tell real from generated samples.
The GAN generator's gradient can vanish early in training when the discriminator confidently rejects generated samples, motivating the non-saturating generator loss used in practice.

Mode collapse in GANs occurs when the generator learns to produce only a limited variety of outputs that fool the discriminator, rather than capturing the full diversity of the real data distribution.
Conditional GANs condition both the generator and discriminator on auxiliary information, such as class labels, allowing controlled generation.

DCGAN established architectural guidelines -- an all-convolutional generator/discriminator, batch normalization, and no fully-connected hidden layers -- that stabilized GAN training for image generation.
Wasserstein GAN replaces the original GAN's Jensen-Shannon-divergence-based loss with an approximation of the Earth Mover's (Wasserstein) distance, improving training stability.
WGAN requires its discriminator (called a critic) to be Lipschitz-continuous, originally enforced via weight clipping, later improved via a gradient penalty.
Pix2Pix uses a conditional GAN with paired training data to learn general-purpose image-to-image translation.
CycleGAN learns image-to-image translation between unpaired domains using a cycle-consistency loss that requires translating an image to the target domain and back to reconstruct the original.

StyleGAN's mapping network transforms a latent code into a style vector, which is injected at multiple resolutions via adaptive instance normalization, giving fine control over generated image attributes at different scales.

Progressive growing trains a GAN by starting at low resolution and progressively adding layers to increase resolution over training, improving stability and quality for high-resolution image synthesis.
Self-Attention GAN adds self-attention layers to GAN generators and discriminators to model long-range spatial dependencies that convolutions alone struggle to capture.
BigGAN showed that scaling up GAN model size and batch size substantially improves the fidelity and diversity of generated images.
Differentiable data augmentation for GANs augments inputs to both real and fake samples, mitigating discriminator overfitting that can otherwise destabilize training.

The GAN discriminator provides a learned, implicit loss function via its classification signal, which helps generators produce sharper, more realistic outputs than models trained with only pixel-wise reconstruction loss.
Training instability in GANs arises in part because the minimax game does not correspond to a simple loss-minimization problem with guaranteed convergence.

Feature matching trains the GAN generator to match statistics of intermediate discriminator features on real data, rather than directly maximizing the discriminator's output on fake data, reducing overtraining on the current discriminator.

entries.paper: Heusel et al. 2017 (FID); Salimans et al. 2016 (Inception Score)
entries.claim: Inception Score and Frechet Inception Distance are commonly used metrics to evaluate GAN-generated image quality and diversity using features from a pretrained image classifier.

Conditional batch normalization and adaptive instance normalization let a GAN generator's normalization statistics be modulated by conditioning information, such as class or style, enabling controllable generation.

Smoothly interpolating between two latent vectors in a trained GAN typically produces a smooth semantic interpolation between the corresponding generated images, suggesting the generator learned a continuous latent manifold.
A Variational Autoencoder learns a probabilistic encoder mapping inputs to a distribution over latent variables, and a decoder reconstructing inputs from latent samples.

The VAE training objective, the evidence lower bound, combines a reconstruction term with a KL-divergence term regularizing the learned latent distribution toward a prior, typically a standard Gaussian.

The VAE reparameterization trick expresses a sampled latent variable as a deterministic function of the input's distribution parameters plus independent noise, allowing gradients to backpropagate through sampling.
VAEs often produce blurrier reconstructions and samples than GANs because their pixel-wise reconstruction loss tends to average over plausible outputs rather than committing to sharp details.
The KL-divergence term in the VAE objective can cause posterior collapse, where the encoder ignores the input and the latent variable becomes uninformative, especially with a powerful decoder.
Beta-VAE upweights the KL-divergence term in the VAE objective to encourage more disentangled latent representations, at some cost to reconstruction quality.
Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models learn to reverse a fixed forward process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to data, generating samples by iteratively denoising from pure noise.
The DDPM forward process is a fixed Markov chain adding a small amount of Gaussian noise at each of many steps, so the data distribution gradually approaches a simple, known noise distribution.
A diffusion model's network is trained to predict the noise added at each forward step, and this predicted noise is used to iteratively denoise a sample during the reverse generation process.
Classifier-free guidance improves conditional diffusion sample quality by combining a conditional and an unconditional model prediction at sampling time, without needing a separate classifier.

entries.paper: Rombach et al. 2022 (Latent Diffusion / Stable Diffusion)
entries.claim: Latent diffusion models run the diffusion process in a lower-dimensional latent space produced by a pretrained autoencoder rather than directly on pixels, substantially reducing compute cost.
Score-based generative models learn the gradient of the log-density of noised data at multiple noise levels, and generate samples via Langevin-dynamics-like sampling.
Denoising diffusion models generally require many sequential sampling steps to generate a single sample, making them slower at inference than single-pass generators like GANs.
DDIM reformulates diffusion sampling as a non-Markovian process that allows deterministic, fewer-step sampling while using the same trained model as DDPM.
Classifier guidance uses gradients from a separately trained classifier on noisy images to steer diffusion sampling toward a desired class, improving sample fidelity to the target label.

entries.paper: Ronneberger et al. 2015; general diffusion practice
entries.claim: U-Net architectures, originally developed for image segmentation, are commonly used as the denoising network backbone in image diffusion models because their encoder-decoder structure with skip connections suits pixel-level prediction.

entries.paper: Rombach et al. 2022; Radford et al. 2021 (CLIP)
entries.claim: Diffusion models can be conditioned on text embeddings, such as from CLIP, via cross-attention layers, enabling text-to-image generation.
The choice of noise schedule, how much noise is added at each forward diffusion step, affects both sample quality and how many reverse steps are needed for good generation.
VAEs provide an explicit, tractable lower-bound likelihood objective, whereas standard GANs do not directly optimize or provide a likelihood estimate for generated data.
Autoregressive image models generate images pixel by pixel, conditioning each pixel's distribution on previously generated pixels, in contrast to the parallel denoising approach of diffusion models.
Reinforcement learning trains an agent to choose actions in an environment to maximize cumulative, typically discounted, reward through trial-and-error interaction rather than labeled examples.
The Markov Decision Process formalism assumes the next state and reward depend only on the current state and action, not on the full history.

Q-learning is an off-policy temporal-difference algorithm that learns the action-value function via bootstrapped updates toward the observed reward plus the discounted maximum Q-value of the next state.
Q-learning is off-policy because it learns the value of the greedy optimal policy while the agent's actual training behavior can follow a different, exploratory policy.
The exploration-exploitation tradeoff in RL balances trying new actions to discover better rewards against choosing the currently best-known action to maximize reward.
Epsilon-greedy exploration selects a random action with probability epsilon and the current best-estimated action otherwise, providing a simple exploration mechanism during RL training.
Deep Q-Networks approximate the Q-function with a deep neural network, enabling Q-learning to scale to high-dimensional inputs like raw pixels, such as Atari games.

DQN's experience replay buffer stores past transitions and samples mini-batches from it randomly, breaking the strong temporal correlations in sequentially-collected RL data and improving training stability.
DQN uses a separate, periodically-updated target network to compute the bootstrapped target Q-value, reducing instability caused by value estimates and targets changing simultaneously.
Policy gradient methods directly parameterize and optimize a stochastic policy via gradient ascent on expected cumulative reward, rather than learning value functions and deriving a policy from them.
REINFORCE estimates the policy gradient using the log-probability of taken actions weighted by the observed return, but suffers from high variance in its gradient estimates.

Subtracting a baseline, such as an estimated state-value function, from the return in policy gradient methods reduces gradient variance without introducing bias, provided the baseline does not depend on the action taken.
Actor-critic methods combine a policy (the actor) with a learned value function (the critic) that provides a lower-variance estimate used to update the actor.
The advantage function, Q(s,a) minus V(s), measures how much better an action is than the average action at a given state, and using it instead of raw returns reduces policy-gradient variance.
The discount factor gamma in an MDP determines how much future rewards are weighted relative to immediate rewards, with gamma closer to 1 giving more weight to long-term reward.

Temporal-difference learning updates value estimates using a bootstrapped target based on the current estimate of the next state's value, rather than waiting for the full episode return like Monte Carlo methods.
On-policy RL algorithms such as SARSA learn the value of the policy currently being followed, including its exploratory actions, unlike off-policy algorithms such as Q-learning.
Function approximation, such as with a neural network, is required to apply RL to environments with large or continuous state/action spaces, where tabular value representations are infeasible.
The deadly triad in RL refers to the instability that can arise when combining function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy learning simultaneously.
AlphaGo combined deep neural networks, policy and value networks, with Monte Carlo Tree Search to defeat top human players at Go, a game previously considered intractable for exhaustive search.
Trust Region Policy Optimization constrains each policy update to stay within a trust region of bounded KL-divergence from the previous policy, preventing destructively large policy updates.
Proximal Policy Optimization approximates TRPO's trust-region constraint with a simpler clipped surrogate objective, making large-scale policy-gradient training easier to implement and tune.
PPO's clipped objective discourages the policy ratio between new and old policy probabilities from moving too far from 1 in a single update, limiting how much the policy can change per step.

Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic runs many parallel actor-learners on different environment copies asynchronously updating a shared model, decorrelating training data without needing an experience replay buffer.
AlphaZero generalized AlphaGo's approach by learning to play Go, chess, and shogi from self-play alone, using no human game data and a single neural network combined with Monte Carlo Tree Search.
Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient extends actor-critic methods to continuous action spaces by learning a deterministic policy and using a critic to provide gradient information for the actor.
Soft Actor-Critic is an off-policy actor-critic algorithm that maximizes both expected reward and policy entropy, encouraging exploration and often improving sample efficiency and robustness.
Reward shaping modifies an RL environment's reward signal, while trying to preserve optimal policies, to provide denser feedback and speed up learning in sparse-reward tasks.

entries.paper: Christiano et al. 2017; Ouyang et al. 2022 (RLHF/InstructGPT)
entries.claim: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback trains a reward model from human preference comparisons, then optimizes a policy against that learned reward model using RL, typically PPO.

InstructGPT showed that fine-tuning a large language model with RLHF produced outputs human raters preferred over a much larger model trained only with standard pretraining and supervised fine-tuning.

Direct Preference Optimization reformulates RLHF's reward-modeling-plus-RL pipeline as a single supervised classification-style loss directly on preference pairs, avoiding explicit reward model training and RL optimization.
Reward hacking occurs when an RL agent finds a way to maximize its specified reward signal that does not correspond to the behavior the reward designer actually intended.

Constitutional AI trains a language model to critique and revise its own outputs according to a set of written principles, then uses the resulting preference data to train the model via RLHF-style methods, reducing reliance on human-labeled harmful examples.

Curriculum learning in RL trains an agent on a sequence of tasks or environments of increasing difficulty, which can speed up learning of complex behaviors compared to training directly on the hardest task.

Hindsight Experience Replay relabels failed trajectories with the goal they actually achieved rather than the intended goal, letting sparse-reward, goal-conditioned RL agents learn from otherwise-useless failed episodes.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning studies settings where multiple learning agents interact in a shared environment, which can be cooperative, competitive, or mixed, and where each agent's optimal policy depends on the others' behavior.
Model-based RL learns an explicit model of the environment's dynamics and can use it to plan or generate synthetic training data, potentially improving sample efficiency over model-free methods.

Offline (batch) RL learns a policy purely from a fixed, previously collected dataset of interactions without further environment interaction, introducing distributional-shift challenges not present in online RL.

entries.paper: Silver et al. 2017; general self-play literature
entries.claim: Self-play, where an agent or population of agents trains by competing against copies or past versions of itself, can produce policies that continually improve without requiring an external opponent or human data.

KL-divergence penalties, as used in PPO for RLHF fine-tuning of language models, constrain the fine-tuned policy to stay close to a reference model, preventing it from drifting too far and degenerating in ways that exploit the reward model.
Language model test loss follows a smooth power-law relationship with model size, dataset size, and compute, over many orders of magnitude.
Under Kaplan et al.'s original scaling analysis, for a fixed compute budget, model performance benefits more from increasing model size than from increasing training data proportionally.

Chinchilla found that many large language models of that era were significantly undertrained relative to their size, and that compute-optimal training requires scaling model size and training tokens roughly equally.
The Chinchilla scaling law implies that, for a fixed compute budget, a smaller model trained on more tokens can outperform a larger model trained on fewer tokens.
Learning rate warmup helps large-batch or large-model training because gradients and updates can be unstable early on, before the model reaches a better-conditioned region of the loss landscape.
Double descent describes test error decreasing, then increasing, then decreasing again as model capacity or training time increases past the classical interpolation threshold.
Grokking describes a model suddenly generalizing well on a task long after it already achieved near-perfect training accuracy, following extended training with weight decay.

The lottery ticket hypothesis posits that a randomly-initialized dense network contains a sparse subnetwork that, trained in isolation from the same initialization, can match the full network's accuracy.
Larger batches give lower-variance stochastic gradient estimates but require more compute per step and can require adjusted learning rates to maintain training dynamics.
Increasing batch size beyond a task-dependent critical threshold yields diminishing returns in training speed per additional compute, since gradient-noise reduction saturates.
Neural scaling laws motivated large-scale pretraining efforts by letting practitioners extrapolate predictable loss improvements before training a full-scale model.

Mixed-precision training uses lower-precision arithmetic, such as FP16 or BF16, for most operations while keeping select operations or a master weight copy in FP32, speeding up training and reducing memory with minimal accuracy loss.

Gradient accumulation simulates a larger effective batch size by summing gradients over several forward/backward passes before a single optimizer step, useful when memory limits the batch size on a single device.
Data parallelism trains identical model replicas on different data shards across multiple devices and synchronizes gradients or parameters between them.
Model parallelism splits a single model's parameters or layers across multiple devices, used when a model is too large to fit in one device's memory.

Pipeline parallelism splits a model into sequential stages placed on different devices, passing activations between stages, and can overlap computation across micro-batches to improve device utilization.
Gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory by recomputing intermediate activations during the backward pass instead of storing all of them during the forward pass.

The compute-optimal frontier for a fixed FLOPs budget specifies the model-size and dataset-size combination that minimizes achievable loss, as characterized empirically by scaling-law studies like Chinchilla.
Overparameterized neural networks, with far more parameters than training examples, can still generalize well in practice, a phenomenon in tension with classical bias-variance tradeoff predictions.
Emergent abilities in large language models refer to capabilities that appear sharply only once model scale crosses a certain threshold, rather than improving smoothly with scale.
LoRA fine-tunes large pretrained models by injecting small trainable low-rank decomposition matrices into existing weight matrices, while keeping the original pretrained weights frozen.

LoRA's low-rank update matrices are added to the frozen pretrained weight during the forward pass, and only these small matrices are trained, drastically reducing trainable parameters compared to full fine-tuning.
QLoRA combines 4-bit quantization of the frozen base model with LoRA adapters, enabling fine-tuning of very large language models on a single consumer-grade GPU.

Adapter modules insert small trainable bottleneck layers between the layers of a frozen pretrained Transformer, allowing task-specific fine-tuning with a small fraction of the full model's parameters.
Prefix tuning prepends a sequence of trainable continuous vectors to the input of each Transformer layer, while keeping the pretrained model's parameters frozen.
Prompt tuning prepends only a small set of trainable continuous embeddings to the input layer, and its effectiveness relative to full fine-tuning improves as model scale increases.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods freeze most of a pretrained model's weights and train only a small number of additional or modified parameters, reducing memory and storage costs compared to full fine-tuning.
Because LoRA only adds small trainable matrices, multiple LoRA adapters for different tasks can be trained and swapped into the same frozen base model without storing multiple full model copies.

In-context learning, unlike parameter-efficient fine-tuning, adapts a frozen model's behavior at inference time purely via examples or instructions in the prompt, without updating any model parameters.

Instruction tuning fine-tunes a pretrained language model on a diverse set of tasks phrased as natural-language instructions, improving its ability to follow novel instructions it was not explicitly trained on.
Full fine-tuning updates all of a pretrained model's parameters on a downstream task, typically achieving strong task performance but requiring a full separate model copy per task.
BitFit fine-tunes only the bias terms of a pretrained Transformer, leaving all weight matrices frozen, and was found to be surprisingly competitive with full fine-tuning on some tasks.
LoRA's rank hyperparameter controls the capacity of the injected low-rank update; higher rank increases trainable parameters and potential expressiveness at higher memory and compute cost.
Adapter-based and LoRA-based fine-tuning can mitigate catastrophic forgetting of the base model's pretrained knowledge, since the original pretrained weights remain unchanged.
Multitask prompt tuning and similar methods learn a shared or transferable set of soft prompts across tasks to improve sample efficiency for new tasks.

Fine-tuning a pretrained model on a narrow downstream dataset can degrade its performance on tasks outside that dataset's distribution, a form of catastrophic forgetting sometimes mitigated with PEFT methods.
IA3 rescales activations in a pretrained Transformer using learned per-channel vectors, introducing very few trainable parameters compared to LoRA or adapters.
Reducing the number of trainable parameters during fine-tuning also reduces the memory needed for optimizer states, such as Adam's per-parameter moment estimates, not just for gradients.
Soft prompts learned via prompt tuning are continuous vectors that do not necessarily correspond to any discrete natural-language token, unlike hand-written discrete prompts.

PEFT methods make it practical to maintain many task-specific or user-specific customizations of a single large pretrained model, since each customization requires storing only a small set of extra parameters.

Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student network to mimic a larger teacher network's output distribution, often using a softened temperature-scaled softmax, transferring learned behavior into a more compact model.

Distillation's temperature parameter softens the teacher's output probability distribution, revealing more information about relative class similarities than the original sharp, near-one-hot predictions.

Network pruning removes individual weights or entire structural units, such as neurons, channels, or filters, from a trained network, reducing its size and, for structured pruning, potentially its inference compute.

Unstructured pruning removes individual weights based on a criterion like magnitude, producing sparse weight matrices that often require specialized hardware or software support to realize actual speedups.
Structured pruning removes entire channels, filters, or layers, producing a smaller dense network that can run faster on standard hardware without special sparse-matrix support.
Iterative magnitude pruning followed by rewinding remaining weights to their early-training values can find very sparse subnetworks that train to match the accuracy of the original dense network.

Quantization reduces the numerical precision used to represent a model's weights and/or activations, such as from 32-bit floating point to 8-bit integers, reducing memory footprint and often speeding up inference.

Post-training quantization converts an already-trained full-precision model to lower precision without further training, while quantization-aware training simulates quantization effects during training to reduce accuracy loss.
Weight clustering groups similar weight values together and stores only cluster indices plus a small codebook, reducing the storage needed for model weights.
Low-rank factorization compresses a weight matrix by approximating it as the product of two smaller matrices, reducing parameter count at the cost of some representational capacity.

Mixed 4-bit/8-bit quantization schemes for large language models often keep a small number of numerically sensitive outlier weights or activations at higher precision to preserve accuracy while quantizing the bulk more aggressively.
Pruning, quantization, and distillation are frequently combined in sequence, since they target different sources of redundancy and their benefits are often complementary.
Structured sparsity patterns designed to match specific hardware accelerators, such as N:M sparsity, can achieve real inference speedups on hardware with native sparse-matrix support.
Early-exit architectures allow easy inputs to skip later network layers and produce a prediction from an intermediate layer, reducing average inference compute at some cost to worst-case accuracy.
Weight sharing, such as ALBERT's cross-layer parameter sharing, reduces a model's total unique parameter count by reusing the same weights across multiple layers or positions.
Distillation can transfer knowledge from an ensemble of teacher models rather than a single teacher, often producing a student that generalizes better than one distilled from a single teacher.

Compressing a model can degrade its performance disproportionately on rare classes or edge cases relative to its overall average accuracy, since compression tends to remove capacity used for less-common patterns first.
Neural network compression for on-device or edge deployment specifically targets reducing memory footprint, inference latency, and energy consumption to meet mobile or embedded hardware constraints.

Progressive or curriculum-based distillation trains a student to match teacher outputs on progressively harder examples or intermediate representations, improving effectiveness for very deep teacher-student capacity gaps.

Compressed models trained via distillation, pruning, or quantization can sometimes match or exceed the accuracy of a directly-trained smaller model of the same final size, benefiting from the larger model's optimization trajectory.
Vision Transformer splits an image into fixed-size patches, linearly embeds each patch, and processes the resulting sequence with a standard Transformer encoder.
ViT requires substantially more pretraining data than CNNs to match or exceed CNN performance, because it lacks convolution's built-in inductive biases like locality and translation equivariance.
A learnable [class] token, prepended to ViT's patch embedding sequence, aggregates global image information through self-attention and is used for final classification.
DeiT showed that Vision Transformers can be trained effectively on much smaller datasets, such as only ImageNet, using strong data augmentation and knowledge distillation from a CNN teacher.

Swin Transformer computes self-attention within local, non-overlapping windows and shifts these windows between successive layers, achieving linear rather than quadratic computational complexity with image size while allowing cross-window information flow.

DETR reformulates object detection as a direct set-prediction problem, using a Transformer encoder-decoder with a fixed set of learned object queries and a bipartite matching loss, removing the need for hand-designed components like anchor boxes and non-maximum suppression.

entries.paper: Ren et al. 2015; Liu et al. 2016 (SSD)
entries.claim: Anchor-based object detectors predict offsets relative to a predefined set of reference boxes of various scales and aspect ratios placed across the image.

Non-maximum suppression is a post-processing step in traditional object detectors that removes duplicate, overlapping bounding-box predictions for the same object, keeping only the highest-confidence box.

Feature Pyramid Networks combine low-resolution, semantically strong features with high-resolution, semantically weak features via a top-down pathway with lateral connections, improving detection of objects at multiple scales.

Masked Autoencoders pretrain a Vision Transformer by masking a large fraction of image patches and training the model to reconstruct the missing pixels, analogous to BERT's masked language modeling for images.
Patch embeddings in ViT are typically produced via a single linear projection, equivalent to a strided convolution, applied to each non-overlapping image patch.

entries.paper: Liu et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2021 (PVT)
entries.claim: Hierarchical vision transformers produce multi-scale feature maps like CNNs, unlike the original ViT which maintains a single fixed resolution throughout its layers, making them more directly usable as backbones for dense prediction tasks.
Convolutional stem layers are sometimes added before a Transformer's patch embedding to introduce local, translation-equivariant inductive bias, improving optimization stability and data efficiency.

CLIP jointly trains an image encoder and a text encoder with a contrastive objective on image-caption pairs, so matching image-text pairs have high embedding similarity and mismatched pairs have low similarity.

CLIP's contrastively trained embeddings enable zero-shot image classification by comparing an image's embedding to the embeddings of natural-language class-name prompts, without task-specific fine-tuning.

Segment Anything trains a promptable segmentation model on a very large mask dataset, allowing it to segment objects in new images given prompts like points or boxes, without task-specific retraining.

Panoptic segmentation unifies semantic segmentation, assigning a class to every pixel, and instance segmentation, distinguishing individual object instances, into a single task and output representation.
Object detection evaluation commonly uses mean Average Precision, which aggregates precision-recall performance across multiple object classes and Intersection-over-Union thresholds.
Intersection over Union measures the overlap between a predicted bounding box or mask and the ground-truth box or mask as the ratio of their intersection area to their union area.

Two-stage object detectors, such as Faster R-CNN, first generate candidate object regions and then classify and refine each region, generally achieving higher accuracy than single-stage detectors like YOLO or SSD at the cost of slower inference.
Contrastive learning trains a model to pull representations of similar (positive) pairs closer together in embedding space while pushing dissimilar (negative) pairs apart.

SimCLR generates positive pairs by applying two random data augmentations to the same image, and trains an encoder plus a projection head with a contrastive loss to make their embeddings similar relative to other images in the batch.
SimCLR's performance improves substantially with larger batch sizes, since larger batches provide more negative examples per training step for the contrastive loss.
MoCo maintains a large, consistent dictionary of negative examples using a momentum-updated encoder and a queue, decoupling the number of negatives from the training batch size.

The momentum encoder in MoCo is updated as a slowly-moving exponential moving average of the main query encoder's parameters, keeping the dictionary of negative keys relatively consistent over training.

BYOL trains a self-supervised representation using only positive pairs, with no explicit negative examples, predicting one augmented view's representation from another using an online network and a slowly-updated target network.
Self-supervised pretraining objectives learn representations from unlabeled data by constructing a supervisory signal directly from the data itself, rather than from human-provided labels.
Masked Autoencoders are a form of self-supervised learning for vision that reconstructs masked-out image patches, analogous to BERT's masked language modeling for text.
Contrastive Predictive Coding learns representations by training a model to predict future latent representations of a sequence from past context, using a contrastive InfoNCE loss.
The InfoNCE loss used in many contrastive learning methods can be interpreted as approximately maximizing a lower bound on the mutual information between two views or an input and its context.
SwAV performs contrastive learning without explicit pairwise comparisons by instead comparing cluster assignments computed online for different augmented views of the same image.
The choice and strength of data augmentations, such as cropping, color distortion, and blurring, has a large effect on the quality of representations learned by contrastive methods like SimCLR.

A small projection head applied after the base encoder is used during contrastive pretraining, and discarding it afterward, using only the base encoder's output for downstream tasks, generally improves downstream performance.
Self-supervised pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning on a smaller labeled dataset often outperforms training the same architecture from scratch on that labeled dataset alone.

CLIP's contrastive pretraining on paired image-text data can be viewed as cross-modal self-supervised learning, since the natural pairing of co-occurring text and images supplies the supervisory signal.
Hard negatives, examples similar to the positive but technically different, provide a stronger contrastive training signal than easy, obviously-dissimilar negatives.
Linear probing evaluates the quality of self-supervised representations by freezing the pretrained encoder and training only a linear classifier on top of its fixed features for a downstream task.

DINO trains a Vision Transformer with a self-distillation objective, where a student network matches the output of a momentum-updated teacher network on different augmented views, without using any labels.

Self-supervised Vision Transformers trained with methods like DINO have been observed to learn attention maps that closely correspond to semantic object boundaries, emerging without any segmentation supervision.

Collapse, where all representations map to the same constant output, is a failure mode that contrastive and self-distillation methods must specifically guard against, using mechanisms like negative examples, stop-gradients, or predictor networks.
Graph Neural Networks learn node representations by iteratively aggregating and transforming information from a node's local neighborhood, a process often called message passing.

The Graph Convolutional Network approximates spectral graph convolutions with a layer-wise propagation rule that aggregates a node's own features with those of its immediate neighbors, normalized by node degree.
GraphSAGE learns an inductive node embedding function by sampling and aggregating features from a fixed-size neighborhood, allowing it to generate embeddings for nodes unseen during training.
Graph Attention Networks learn attention weights over a node's neighbors, allowing the network to weigh neighbor contributions unequally rather than using fixed degree-based normalization as in GCN.

Message passing neural networks generalize many GNN variants into a common framework of message computation, aggregation such as sum, mean, or max, and node-state update functions applied over multiple rounds.

Over-smoothing in GNNs refers to node representations becoming indistinguishable from each other as the number of message-passing layers increases, since repeated neighborhood averaging washes out node-specific information.
GNNs are naturally suited to non-Euclidean, irregularly structured data such as social networks, molecules, and citation graphs, where CNNs' fixed grid structure does not directly apply.
Graph pooling operations aggregate node-level representations into a single graph-level representation, analogous to how pooling in CNNs reduces spatial resolution, for graph-level prediction tasks.
Message passing GNNs are provably no more powerful at distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs than the Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test, a result formalized by the Graph Isomorphism Network.
GIN uses a sum aggregator, rather than mean or max, for neighbor features, which the authors show is necessary to match the discriminative power of the Weisfeiler-Lehman test.
Heterogeneous graph neural networks handle graphs with multiple node types and/or edge types, often using type-specific transformation or attention parameters.

Graph neural networks are used for molecular property prediction by representing atoms as nodes and chemical bonds as edges, letting the network learn representations that respect molecular structure.
Knowledge graph embedding methods learn vector representations of entities and relations such that a scoring function applied to head-relation-tail triples reflects whether the triple is likely true.
TransE models a relation as a translation in embedding space, aiming for the embedding of the head entity plus the relation to be close to the embedding of the tail entity for true triples.
Graph neural networks can suffer from over-squashing, where information from distant nodes must be compressed through narrow graph paths, bottlenecking long-range information propagation.

Spatial-temporal graph neural networks combine graph convolutions for spatial or relational structure with recurrent or temporal convolution layers for time dependence, used for tasks like traffic forecasting.

Graph neural networks applied to citation or social networks typically use semi-supervised node classification, where labels are known for only a subset of nodes and the model propagates information from labeled to unlabeled nodes via graph structure.
Edge features can be incorporated into message-passing GNNs by conditioning message computation on the attributes of the edge connecting two nodes, in addition to node features.

Graph Neural Networks have been used to approximate combinatorial optimization and physical simulation problems by learning to predict quantities on a graph-structured representation of the underlying system.
Relational Graph Convolutional Networks extend GCNs to multi-relational graphs, such as knowledge graphs, by using relation-specific transformation weights for each edge type.

Xavier/Glorot initialization sets initial weight variance based on the number of input and output units of a layer, aiming to keep activation and gradient variance roughly constant across layers at the start of training.
He initialization adjusts Xavier-style initialization to account for ReLU activations zeroing out roughly half their inputs, keeping activation variance stable in deep ReLU networks.
Poor weight initialization can cause activations or gradients to vanish or explode as they propagate through many layers, especially in deep networks without normalization or residual connections.
Batch normalization reduces sensitivity to weight initialization scale, since it renormalizes activations at each layer regardless of incoming weight magnitudes.
Layer normalization computes normalization statistics across the feature dimension of a single training example, rather than across the batch dimension as batch normalization does.
Instance normalization normalizes each individual feature channel of each individual example separately, and is commonly used in style-transfer and image generation models.

Group normalization divides channels into groups and normalizes within each group per example, providing performance closer to batch normalization at small batch sizes where batch statistics become unreliable.
Weight normalization reparameterizes a weight vector into a magnitude scalar and a direction vector, decoupling optimization of a weight's length from its direction.

Residual connections mitigate vanishing gradients by allowing gradients to flow through an identity path in addition to the transformed path, so gradients need not pass through every nonlinear transformation to reach earlier layers.

Normalization layers are typically placed either before (pre-norm) or after (post-norm) the main sub-layer transformation in a residual block, with pre-norm generally giving more stable gradients at greater depth.

Batch normalization computes different statistics at training time, using batch statistics, versus inference time, using a running average accumulated during training, which can cause train/inference discrepancies if batch statistics are poorly estimated.

Proper weight initialization aims for activations to neither saturate nonlinearities like sigmoid or tanh nor grow or shrink exponentially in magnitude as they pass through successive layers of an untrained network.

Orthogonal initialization sets initial weight matrices to be approximately orthogonal, which can help preserve the norm of signals and gradients through many layers, particularly in deep or recurrent networks.
Fixup initialization shows that very deep residual networks can be trained without any normalization layers at all, using a carefully designed initialization scheme instead.
Normalization layers introduce learnable scale and shift parameters after normalizing, allowing the network to recover a non-normalized representation if that minimizes the loss.
Batch normalization's dependence on batch composition makes its training-time and evaluation-time behavior differ, a discrepancy that is more pronounced for small batch sizes.

RMSNorm simplifies layer normalization by normalizing using only the root-mean-square of activations, omitting the mean-centering step, and is used in several modern large language model architectures.

Deep networks without any normalization or careful initialization scheme were historically very difficult to train past a moderate depth, motivating specialized initialization schemes and normalization layers.
The choice of activation function interacts with initialization scheme, since variances derived assuming linear or ReLU activations may not be optimal for other nonlinearities like GELU or Swish.

Computing normalization statistics per-sample, as in layer normalization, rather than per-batch, as in batch normalization, makes training behavior independent of batch size, useful when batch sizes vary or are very small.

Cross-entropy loss for classification measures the difference between a predicted probability distribution over classes and the true label distribution, penalizing confident incorrect predictions heavily.
Minimizing cross-entropy loss for a classifier is equivalent to performing maximum likelihood estimation under the assumption that the model outputs a categorical probability distribution.
Mean squared error loss for regression penalizes the squared difference between predicted and true continuous values, and is sensitive to outliers due to the squaring of errors.
Mean absolute error is less sensitive to outliers than mean squared error because it penalizes errors linearly rather than quadratically.

Focal loss down-weights the loss contribution of easy, well-classified examples, focusing training on hard, misclassified examples, which helps address extreme class imbalance in tasks like object detection.

Precision measures the fraction of positive predictions that are actually correct, while recall measures the fraction of actual positives correctly identified, with a general tradeoff between the two as a decision threshold varies.
The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a single metric that balances both, particularly useful when class distributions are imbalanced.

Accuracy as an evaluation metric can be misleading on imbalanced datasets, since a model that always predicts the majority class can achieve high accuracy while having zero recall on minority classes.
The area under the ROC curve summarizes a binary classifier's ability to rank positive examples higher than negative examples across all possible decision thresholds.

Perplexity, commonly used to evaluate language models, is the exponentiated average negative log-likelihood the model assigns to a held-out token sequence, with lower perplexity indicating a better-fitting model.
BLEU evaluates machine translation output by measuring n-gram overlap between the generated translation and one or more human reference translations, with a brevity penalty for overly short outputs.
ROUGE evaluates text summarization output primarily by measuring recall-oriented n-gram or longest-common-subsequence overlap between generated and reference summaries.

Contrastive losses such as triplet loss and InfoNCE explicitly optimize relative distances between an anchor, a positive example, and one or more negative examples in embedding space, rather than an absolute per-example target.

Hinge loss penalizes predictions that are correct but insufficiently confident, within a margin, not just incorrect predictions, and is used in support vector machines and some neural network classifiers.

KL-divergence measures how one probability distribution diverges from a reference distribution, and is used both as a training loss, such as in VAEs, and as an evaluation or regularization tool, such as in RLHF fine-tuning.

Calibration of a probabilistic classifier refers to whether its predicted confidence scores match the actual empirical frequency of correctness; a well-calibrated model predicting 80% confidence should be correct about 80% of the time on such predictions.
Class-imbalanced classification tasks often use metrics like precision, recall, F1, or balanced accuracy instead of raw accuracy, since raw accuracy can hide poor performance on minority classes.
Word Error Rate, used to evaluate speech recognition systems, measures the edit distance between the predicted transcript and the reference transcript, normalized by reference length.
Exact match and token-level F1 are common evaluation metrics for extractive question answering, comparing a predicted answer span against one or more ground-truth answer spans.

Human evaluation, such as pairwise preference judgments, is often used for open-ended generation tasks like dialogue or summarization, since automatic metrics like BLEU or ROUGE often correlate poorly with human judgments of quality for such tasks.
Mixture-of-Experts models route each input to a subset of specialized expert sub-networks, using a learned gating function, activating only a fraction of the model's total parameters per input.

Sparsely-gated Mixture-of-Experts layers select only the top-k highest-scoring experts per input token via a learned gating network, keeping computation roughly constant even as total parameter count grows with the number of experts.
Mixture-of-Experts models can scale total parameter count substantially while keeping compute cost per input token roughly fixed, since only a small subset of experts activates for any given input.

Switch Transformer simplifies Mixture-of-Experts routing by sending each token to exactly one expert, top-1 routing, rather than multiple experts, reducing routing computation and communication overhead.

entries.paper: Shazeer et al. 2017; Fedus et al. 2021
entries.claim: Load balancing losses are added during Mixture-of-Experts training to encourage the gating network to distribute tokens roughly evenly across experts, preventing a small subset of experts from being overused.
GShard demonstrated large-scale Mixture-of-Experts training by sharding experts across many accelerator devices, with automatic partitioning and communication for the routing step.

Mixture-of-Experts models can suffer from training instability, including expert collapse, where the gating network routes most or all tokens to only a few experts, undermining intended specialization.

Because only a subset of experts activates per token, Mixture-of-Experts models typically achieve better quality-per-training-FLOP than equivalently-sized dense models, though they require more total memory to store all expert parameters.
Expert capacity in Mixture-of-Experts implementations sets a maximum number of tokens each expert can process per batch; tokens exceeding this limit are typically dropped or passed through unchanged.

Conditional computation, of which Mixture-of-Experts is one instance, refers to architectures where different parts of the network activate depending on the input, rather than always executing the entire network.

Mixture-of-Experts routing decisions are typically discrete, which makes the routing function non-differentiable and requires techniques like straight-through estimators or auxiliary losses to train the gating network end-to-end.
Mixture-of-Experts models increase communication overhead in distributed training because tokens must often be routed via all-to-all communication to the device holding their assigned expert.
Sparse Mixture-of-Experts models have been used to scale large language models to far more total parameters than would be feasible with a dense architecture under the same training compute budget.

Hash-based routing assigns tokens to experts using a fixed hash function rather than a learned gating network, avoiding routing instabilities at the cost of losing input-dependent adaptivity in expert assignment.
Mixture-of-Experts models can in principle be converted to a dense model at inference time by activating all experts, but this defeats the compute-saving purpose of sparse activation.

Auxiliary load-balancing losses in Mixture-of-Experts training are typically added to the main task loss with a small weighting coefficient, trading off perfect load balance against not distorting the primary training objective.

Expert specialization in trained Mixture-of-Experts models is not always semantically interpretable; experts do not necessarily correspond to intuitive categories even when routing is learned end-to-end.

Mixture-of-Experts architectures have been used in some of the largest publicly known language models as a way to increase model capacity without proportionally increasing inference compute per token.

Fine-tuning Mixture-of-Experts models can be more prone to overfitting on small downstream datasets than equivalent dense models, since routing decisions can overfit to the fine-tuning data's distribution.

Top-k routing with k greater than 1, where each token is processed by multiple experts and outputs are combined, can improve quality relative to top-1 routing, at the cost of proportionally more compute per token.
Neural Architecture Search automates the design of neural network architectures by searching over a defined space of possible architectures to find one that performs well on a target task.

Early Neural Architecture Search methods used reinforcement learning, training a controller network to generate architecture descriptions and updating it based on the resulting trained architecture's validation performance.
NAS with reinforcement learning historically required training many candidate architectures from scratch to evaluate them, making the search process extremely computationally expensive.

Weight-sharing NAS methods dramatically reduce search cost by training a single large supernet containing all candidate architectures as subgraphs, sharing weights across candidates instead of training each from scratch.

DARTS relaxes the discrete architecture search space into a continuous one by taking a weighted combination of candidate operations, allowing architecture search via gradient descent rather than reinforcement learning or evolutionary search.
Evolutionary algorithms for NAS maintain a population of candidate architectures, iteratively mutating and selecting the best-performing ones based on validation performance.
EfficientNet's compound scaling was derived by using neural architecture search to find a good baseline architecture, then applying a principled scaling rule across depth, width, and resolution.
AutoML broadly refers to automating parts of the machine learning pipeline beyond architecture search, including hyperparameter tuning, feature engineering, and data preprocessing choices.

Hyperparameter optimization methods such as random search, Bayesian optimization, and Hyperband search over settings like learning rate, batch size, and regularization strength to maximize validation performance.

Random search over hyperparameters has been shown to often outperform manual tuning and even grid search for a given compute budget, exploring hyperparameter combinations more efficiently than an exhaustive grid.
Bayesian optimization builds a probabilistic surrogate model of the relationship between hyperparameters and validation performance, using it to select promising configurations to evaluate next.

Hyperband allocates compute budget adaptively by running many hyperparameter configurations for a short time and progressively eliminating poorly-performing ones, allocating more budget to promising configurations.

Neural Architecture Search's search space design, the set of allowed operations and connectivity patterns, substantially affects both the quality of discovered architectures and the computational feasibility of the search.

Proxy tasks, such as training on a smaller dataset or for fewer epochs, are often used during architecture search to estimate an architecture's quality more cheaply, at the risk that proxy-task rankings do not always transfer to the full-scale task.

Once-for-all networks train a single large network that can be specialized into many smaller sub-networks for different deployment constraints, such as latency or memory, without retraining from scratch.
NAS-discovered architectures for image classification often contain irregular, non-intuitive connectivity patterns that differ substantially from architectures designed by human experts.
Multi-objective NAS optimizes for multiple criteria simultaneously, such as accuracy and inference latency or model size, producing a Pareto front of architectures trading off these objectives.

Transferability of NAS-discovered architectures and hyperparameters across datasets and tasks is not guaranteed, since an architecture optimized for one dataset's characteristics may not be optimal for a substantially different dataset.

AutoML systems for tabular data commonly automate model selection among algorithms like gradient boosting, random forests, and neural networks, in addition to hyperparameter tuning for each candidate.

The high computational cost of naive NAS approaches, training many full architectures from scratch, motivated substantial research into cheaper proxies, weight sharing, and one-shot search methods to make architecture search practical for individual researchers.
Federated learning trains a shared model across many decentralized devices or clients holding local data, without directly transferring that raw data to a central server.
Federated Averaging trains a global model by having clients perform several local SGD steps on their own data, then averaging the resulting client model updates on a central server.
Federated learning's core motivation is data privacy: raw user data never leaves the client device, only model updates such as gradients or weights are communicated.

Non-IID data across clients, where each client's local data distribution differs from the overall population, is a major federated learning challenge, since it can cause client updates to conflict and slow or destabilize convergence.

Communication cost, not just computation, is often the primary bottleneck in federated learning, since model updates must be transmitted repeatedly over potentially slow or unreliable network connections.
Secure aggregation protocols allow a federated learning server to compute the sum or average of client updates without being able to inspect any individual client's update.
Differential privacy can be incorporated into federated learning by adding calibrated noise to client updates or aggregated updates, providing formal privacy guarantees at some cost to model utility.

Data parallelism, unlike federated learning, typically assumes data is centrally accessible and IID-shuffled across workers, whereas federated learning's clients retain private, often non-IID, local data.

All-reduce is a common communication pattern in synchronous distributed data-parallel training that efficiently sums or averages gradients across all worker devices without a single central bottleneck node.

Asynchronous distributed training allows workers to push gradient updates to a parameter server without waiting for other workers to finish, improving hardware utilization at the cost of potentially using stale gradients computed from an outdated model version.
Parameter servers store the canonical copy of model parameters and handle read/write requests from distributed workers during large-scale distributed training.
Federated learning clients are typically not available simultaneously, such as mobile devices, so training rounds usually sample only a subset of available clients to participate in each round.

Client drift in federated learning refers to local client models diverging significantly from each other during local training on non-IID data, which averaging must then reconcile, sometimes degrading global model quality.
FedProx adds a proximal term to each client's local objective, penalizing deviation from the current global model, to mitigate client drift under non-IID data and heterogeneous client compute.

Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices, such as within a single Transformer layer, across multiple devices, allowing very large layers to be computed collaboratively rather than requiring a single device to hold the full layer.
Distributed training frameworks combine data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism, so-called 3D parallelism, to train models whose size exceeds what any single strategy alone can efficiently support.

ZeRO reduces the memory redundancy of standard data-parallel training by partitioning optimizer states, gradients, and optionally parameters across data-parallel workers instead of replicating them on every worker.
Straggler mitigation techniques in distributed training address the problem that some workers consistently finish computation more slowly than others, potentially bottlenecking synchronous training.

Split learning divides a neural network's layers between a client and a server, with the client computing early layers and sending intermediate activations to the server for remaining computation, offloading some compute from resource-constrained clients.

Cross-silo federated learning, such as between hospitals or banks, typically involves a small number of reliable, high-compute participants, in contrast to cross-device federated learning, which involves a huge number of unreliable, low-compute participants.
Saliency maps visualize which input pixels or features most influence a model's prediction, typically by computing the gradient of the output with respect to the input.
